name: Functional fixedness
statement: Using an object for its ordinary purpose, in the minutes before a problem needs it for something else, makes that second use harder to find.
meaning: Karl Duncker's claim is narrow and it is about one object inside one problem. A tool that has just been used in its usual function is less available for an unusual one, even when it lies in plain sight on the table. Duncker called this heterogeneous functional fixedness, meaning fixedness produced by a function unlike the one now demanded. His test was not a puzzle given cold. Each problem was given in two settings, once with the crucial object already pressed into its normal job and once with that job done some other way, so that the only thing varying was the object's recent history. The measure was whether the person reached the solution that used the crucial object. Duncker's own summary of the result: 'the object which is not fixed is almost twice as easily found as the object which is fixed'. The claim does not say the person forgets the object exists, and it does not say the effect grows with expertise or with age.

origin.note: The monograph is Lynne S. Lees's English translation of Duncker's 1935 book Zur Psychologie des produktiven Denkens, prepared after his death. Wolfgang Köhler's introductory note records that the German original had become 'virtually unobtainable'. Duncker's own foreword is dated Berlin, February 1935. Chapter VII names and tests functional fixedness. The candle problem everyone quotes is Duncker's box problem, and in his version three candles are fixed to a door using three small pasteboard boxes.

evidence: Duncker ran five problems: gimlet, box, pliers, weight and paperclip. In each, the crucial object was either used first in its ordinary function or not, and it lay among a clutter of other objects, none better suited to the solution. He alternated the two settings within each person, one half taking the series as without, after, without, after, without, and the other half in the reverse, so that the comparison did not ride on differences between individuals. The arithmetic mean of the five solution rates was 97.1% without prior use and 58.2% with it. The box problem showed the widest gap, 7 of 7 against 3 of 7, and the weight problem the narrowest, 12 of 12 against 9 of 12. Cell sizes ran from 7 to 15 people. A second experiment, on the box and on a sixth cork problem, reversed Duncker's own prediction. He expected that filling the boxes with buttons rather than with the candles, matches and tacks the problem needed would loosen the fixedness, since the prior function would then be peripheral to the situation. Solutions fell instead, from 3 of 7 to 1 of 7 for the box and from 1 of 7 to 0 of 7 for the cork. Duncker attributed the reversal to contact: the box holding the candles is emptied first, and that handling partly offsets the fixing. The developmental result is the one that constrains theory. Tim German and Margaret Anne Defeyter gave 60 children a box that had to become a step rather than a container. Seven-year-olds produced the box solution 40% of the time when the other objects had been presented inside it and 89% when they sat beside it, Fisher's exact test p = .04. That 89% is 8 of 9, one child's data having been dropped for experimenter error. Five-year-olds showed no gap in solution time, U = 21, not significant, and solved the primed version faster than either older group. Defeyter and German repeated this with 120 children on a tube task and again with 120 more on objects the children had never seen, whose functions were taught in the session. With novel objects, 6-year-olds chose the target object first 35% of the time when its taught function had been shown and 95% when it had not, and 7-year-olds 40% against 80%. Five-year-olds sat at 75% in both conditions. Equalising experience did not remove the age difference, which is evidence against experience alone as the cause. German and Barrett took the box task and a spoon task to 29 Shuar aged 12 to 25 in two Ecuadorian villages, a setting with few specialised artefacts. Withdrawals left 28 people analysed on the box problem and 27 on the spoon. On the spoon task the primed group was slower both to pick up the spoon and to finish, U = 51.0 and U = 47.5, one-tailed ps < .05. On the box task the selection difference reached U = 63, p = .056 one-tailed, and the solution-time difference did not separate the groups, U = 71.5.

replication.headline: Robert Adamson repeated three of Duncker's problems with 57 people and proper control groups, and 41% solved the box problem after using the boxes as containers against 86% who had not.

study.cite: Adamson, R. E. (1952). Functional fixedness as related to problem solving: a repetition of three experiments. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 44(4), 288-291.

replication.detail: Adamson's subjects were college students, 29 in the pre-utilisation group and 28 in the control. On the box problem, 12 of 29 solved against 24 of 28, chi-square 12.0, p = .001, and only 7 of the primed group finished faster than the combined median against 22 of the control, chi-square 14.8, p = .001. The gimlet problem defeated only three people, all of them primed, so solution counts could not separate the groups; across the 54 who solved it, mean time was 246.6 seconds against 144.0, t' = 3.71, p = .001. Everyone solved the paperclip problem, at 107.9 seconds against 63.0, t' = 2.38, p = .01. Tests were one-tailed. Adamson wrote that Duncker had carried his experiments through 'with but 14 Ss and under poorly specified experimental conditions'. That count does not survive Duncker's own Table 3, which lists 12 subjects in each setting of the weight problem alone. Adamson judged his own subjects the abler group, and found that performance on one primed problem barely predicted performance on another: of the three pairwise tests, only box against paperclip reached p < .05, and he concluded that a single primed problem is not a reliable measure of individual susceptibility. The developmental finding has been repeated by its own authors, in the 2003 paper above and in two further replications reported inside the 2000 paper, 100 children in total and presented as a conference poster, where 5-year-olds solved at 64% primed and 65% unprimed while the 7-year-old group fell from 89% to 18%. Sonja Ebel and colleagues carried the design to chimpanzees in 2024. Sixteen apes at Leipzig Zoo either drank juice through a hose or handled the same hose without drinking, then had to poke food from a tube with it. As many solved the task either way, 5 of 8 against 8 of 8, Fisher's exact test p = 0.200, but the drinking group took longer to solve it, chi-square 7.33, p = 0.007, and longer to pull the hose out of the drinking container, chi-square 8.26, p = 0.004. The gap was still there nine months later. A second study on 14 apes induced the prior function by letting them watch another chimpanzee drink, and that group found the solution strategy less often, chi-square 5.23, p = 0.022. Deborah Kelemen's 2001 paper, given at the Society for Research in Child Development and described by Defeyter and German as a failure to replicate the 2000 result, was not obtained: searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the open web on 17 August 2026 turned up no published version.

limits: The effect is a delay and a reduced rate, not a blockage. In Adamson's paperclip problem every single person solved it, primed or not, and the two mean times were 107.9 seconds and 63.0. Sizes vary by problem for reasons nobody has reduced to a rule: Duncker's weight problem went from 12 of 12 to 9 of 12 while his box problem went from 7 of 7 to 3 of 7, and his own attempt to isolate the mechanism, by swapping relevant filling for neutral filling, produced the opposite of what he predicted. Adamson concluded that achievement on a single primed problem is not a reliable measure of individual susceptibility. Two papers wanted here were not obtained, the position on 17 August 2026. Glucksberg and Weisberg's 1966 study of labelling returns 403 at the American Psychological Association, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, the Internet Archive holds no scan of that volume, and no number from it is quoted on this page. Adamson's own paper is closed at the same publisher, which answers with a bot challenge rather than a paywall page; its text and both tables were read from a transcription hosted at All About Psychology, where the two tables are photographs of the printed page. The DTIC technical report carrying the same work, AD0006119, exists in DTIC's catalogue and answers 'The request is blocked' with HTTP 403 to this session, and the legacy dtic.mil address returns 503, so it was not used. Duncker's monograph was read from the Internet Archive's scan of Psychological Monographs volume 58, issue 5. The cross-cultural evidence rests on one study of 29 people, 28 of whom completed the box problem and 27 the spoon, and its authors report two-tailed probabilities of .033 and .054 for the two spoon measures while giving the box selection difference only as p = .056 one-tailed. No meta-analysis of functional fixedness was located in searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the open web on 17 August 2026, so there is no pooled estimate to quote and no effect-size fields on this entry.
misreadings: The candle problem is usually retold as one candle and one box of tacks, with the box to be tacked to the wall as a shelf. Duncker's box problem uses three candles, three pasteboard boxes and a door, and the three boxes are pinned up as three platforms. Adamson's version melts wax to stick each candle to its box. The second error is the direction of development. Fixedness is widely taught as a habit that thickens with experience, and the measured pattern is that 5-year-olds do not show it, 6- and 7-year-olds do, and the 5-year-olds beat both older groups on the primed version. Defeyter and German's second experiment removed the experience explanation by teaching every child the same new functions for objects none of them had met, and the age difference survived. The third error is to fold Maier's two-string problem in as another demonstration. Maier varied hints rather than prior use: R. Eric Landrum, describing the 1931 study, reports that 39.3% of Maier's 61 subjects produced the pendulum solution unaided, after which those who failed were nudged with a swinging cord and then handed a pair of pliers. Landrum ran the design himself twice, on 64 students and then on 96. Telling people outright to think of a pendulum worked both times. Swinging the cord silently during the instructions did not separate from control in either experiment, and on the two combined it only approached significance, chi-square 5.30, p = .07. That is a study about transfer from a cue, not about an object spoiled by its own recent use. The law of the instrument, at no. 95, and déformation professionnelle, at no. 181, are claims about which problems a person takes on at all, not about one object lying on the table.

sources.text: Duncker, K. (1945). On problem-solving. Psychological Monographs, 58(5, Whole No. 270), i-113. Translated by Lynne S. Lees. Chapter VII carries the five problems, Table 3 the solution rates and Table 4 the neutral-filling reversal. Read here from the Internet Archive's scan of the issue.

Adamson, R. E. (1952). Functional fixedness as related to problem solving: a repetition of three experiments. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 44(4), 288-291. Closed at the American Psychological Association, which answers 403 with a bot challenge. The text and both tables quoted above were read from a transcription published by All About Psychology, not from the journal; its tables are photographs of the printed page, downloaded and read twice. Note that German and Defeyter's reference list gives the pages as 288-293, and Crossref and German and Barrett give 288-291.

German, T. P., & Defeyter, M. A. (2000). Immunity to functional fixedness in young children. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 7(4), 707-712. Source of the 60-child box task, of Table 1, and of the two further replications on 100 children reported in its discussion and cited there as a poster given at the British Psychological Society Cognitive Section conference.

Defeyter, M. A., & German, T. P. (2003). Acquiring an understanding of design: evidence from children's insight problem solving. Cognition, 89(2), 133-155. Source of the two 120-child experiments, including the novel-object test. Read from the authors' copy on the University of California, Santa Barbara server.

German, T. P., & Barrett, H. C. (2005). Functional fixedness in a technologically sparse culture. Psychological Science, 16(1), 1-5. Source of the Shuar figures and of the two-tailed probabilities given in its footnote 3.

Glucksberg, S., & Weisberg, R. W. (1966). Verbal behavior and problem solving: some effects of labeling in a functional fixedness problem. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 71(5), 659-664. Named here because the labelling manipulation belongs in this literature. Not read: the DOI redirects to the American Psychological Association and returns 403, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar record no open copy, the Internet Archive has no scan of the volume, and the PubMed record carries no abstract. No figure from it appears above.

Landrum, R. E. (1990). Maier's (1931) two-string problem revisited: evidence for spontaneous transfer? Psychological Reports, 67(3, Suppl.), 1079-1088. Source of Maier's 1931 figures, which are quoted here at one remove, and of Landrum's own two experiments.

Ebel, S. J., Völter, C. J., Sánchez-Amaro, A., Helming, K. A., Herrmann, E., & Call, J. (2024). Functional fixedness in chimpanzees. Scientific Reports, 14, 12155. Source of the two chimpanzee studies, the nine-month delay and the conspecific-demonstration condition. Every figure above was read from the article's JATS XML at Europe PMC, record PMC11130300.
